about: What this member said on the floor, from the Congressional Record: their own words only, and of those the sentences that name an alignment question's phrases or make a commitment. Written by npm run record:collect (scripts/collect-record.mjs).
name: Cleo Fields

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: EXPRESSING GRATITUDE AND APPRECIATION
statements.title: EXPRESSING GRATITUDE AND APPRECIATION
sentences: To the staff of this institution, the clerks, the Capitol Police, the Parliamentarians, and everyone who keeps this House running, I thank you as well.
I am very disappointed in the Supreme Court's decision in the Louisiana v. Callais case that literally gutted the Voting Rights Act.
And in the case from Louisiana called Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896, where the Supreme Court--this Supreme Court--basically said separate but equal was okay, and they codified it.
Will you treat diversity, equity, and inclusion policies as a way to match talent to opportunity?

Utilize every tool at your disposal to address the affordability crisis at the grocery store, end the war in Iran, bring gas prices down, expand access to healthcare, end childhood poverty, and restore accountability to the executive branch of government.
I will depart again soon because of another Court ruling that the district that I currently represent is an unconstitutional racial gerrymander.
I will keep working for the people I love and for the State that I am still so proud of.
I will keep believing that the arc of the moral universe is a long, long road, but it bends toward justice.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: GIVING VOICE TO DIVERSITY, EQUITY, AND INCLUSION PRINCIPLES
statements.title: GIVING VOICE TO DIVERSITY, EQUITY, AND INCLUSION PRINCIPLES
sentences: The late Sylvester Turner and I were sitting right on this floor, and the gentleman from Illinois invited us to be a part of the Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Caucus.
When the President signed an executive order to do away with diversity, equity, and inclusion, it was, in my view, totally wrong, and I think people need to stand up for what they really believe in.
We need to talk about what is good about diversity, equity, and inclusion and not talk about all of these scare tactics that we have heard from people all across the country.
Businesses across America have decided to end their diversity, equity, and inclusion programs as a result of the Executive Order No. 14151 signed by the President on January 20, 2025.
There was a time in this country that Blacks weren't able to even register to vote.
Mr. Speaker, I urge the gentleman from Illinois to keep on fighting for diversity, equity, and inclusion because it is not a bad thing.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: ENDING OF DEI PROGRAMS THROUGH EXECUTIVE ORDER
statements.title: ENDING OF DEI PROGRAMS THROUGH EXECUTIVE ORDER
sentences: That executive order ended all DEI programs.
The argument that DEI initiatives constitute reverse discrimination fundamentally misunderstands both the history and the purpose of these programs.
DEI initiatives emerged as thoughtful, evidence-based responses to documented inequities suffered by rural communities, minorities, women, the poor, and the disabled.
When the landmark Supreme Court decisions in 2023 and 2024 further restricted race- conscious university admissions and workplace policies, they accelerated a retreat from this understanding.
The history of DEI efforts in America is not some partisan agenda.
Let me be clear: Diversity, equity, and inclusion are not about guarantees and preferences; they are about removing barriers.
When our military, for example, embraced diversity and inclusion, it didn't become weaker.
Mr. Speaker, I yield to the gentleman from Illinois (Mr. Jackson), the chairman of diversity, equity, and inclusion.

Mr. Speaker, one of the problems I think that many people have with DEI programs--which is one of the same problems they had with affirmative action, if you recall--they viewed it as two parallel lines, where you took a person who was less qualified and you elevated him to the level of somebody who was more qualified.
People need to view it as: Everybody in the circle is qualified, but DEI comes in and grabs people who are not chosen only because of the color of their skin or because of their sex.
What is interesting is when the President signed that executive order to do away with three words: diversity, equity, and inclusion, it sent universities in a tailspin.
He said that it was a DEI program, and then later he reversed it.
There are businesses that have ended their DEI programs simply because of that executive order.
The world is always watching us to see what we will accomplish, but now more than ever before, they are watching us to see who we will become.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: DISAPPROVING THE RULE SUBMITTED BY THE BUREAU OF CONSUMER FINANCIAL PROTECTION RELATING TO "OVERDRAFT LENDING: VERY LARGE FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS"
statements.title: DISAPPROVING THE RULE SUBMITTED BY THE BUREAU OF CONSUMER FINANCIAL PROTECTION RELATING TO "OVERDRAFT LENDING: VERY LARGE FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS"
sentences: They are using them to pad their already substantial bottom lines at the expense of working families in Louisiana and across America.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to oppose S.J. Res. 18 which would dismantle important protections against predatory overdraft practices.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: FIGHTING VOTER SUPPRESSION
statements.title: FIGHTING VOTER SUPPRESSION
sentences: Despite all men and women having the full Federal right to vote by 1920, States still devised schemes to impose draconian restrictions to prevent voter registration for people of color.
I was leading folk to the polls to register to vote, and I tried to get my grandmother to go.
Let me just tell you a story.'' She went to register to vote, and they gave her a literacy test.
I finally got her to register to vote, and she voted until she passed.
They gave them tests like citizen tests, voucher tests.
One of the first successes we have had in the battle of voting rights was in 1944 with the Supreme Court decision of Smith v. Allwright when they outlawed White-only primaries.
Following this decision, Black voter registration went up.

Last year, I served as a member of the Louisiana State Senate, and several attempts were made to make it more difficult on a State level for people to register to vote: S. 226 dealt with absentee ballots, and it required you to put your mother's maiden name on your voter application or your vote would be thrown out.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, Congress should advance legislation like the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act and the Freedom to Vote Act to increase equal access across the voting ballot.
I will take a moment of personal privilege to talk about that subsection because it really affected me.
